title: Unsquared ambient displacement is different
subtitle: G2 lecture 133000 · baseline companion · needs expansion
adaptation: First-pass source-derived outline. Section excerpts and any vector equation come from the spoken lecture and its display-only mathematics appendix. Expand with worked mathematics, proofs and topic-specific diagrams.

slides.title: The problem and its setting
slides.lead: Section Four of Davis and Kahan investigates how to transport one subspace onto another.
body: Restricted displacement and squared whole-space displacement admit valid direct-rotation optimality statements, but the printed claim about every unitarily invariant norm of unsquared whole-space displacement fails. A four-dimensional construction makes the distinction explicit. The proposition as printed proposes a threshold of sixty degrees in the real case.

slides.title: Define the ambient transport problem
slides.lead: Take a real Euclidean space and two subspaces U and V of the same dimension.
body: A competitor is an orthogonal matrix W satisfying W U equals V. For a chosen unitarily invariant norm N, measure its cost by N of identity minus W, acting on the entire ambient space. The canonical direct rotation D is one feasible competitor. On each principal plane it turns the source direction into the target direction through the prescribed principal angle, while choosing a compatible action on the perpendicular direction. It therefore has easily computed displacement singular values. The optimization is not over the principal angles. The subspaces and their principal angles are fixed.

slides.title: Why sixty degrees arises in the plane
slides.lead: Let U and V be real lines meeting at a principal angle theta between zero and ninety degrees.
body: An orthogonal transporter of the plane taking U onto V belongs to an orientation-preserving or orientation-reversing component. Each component has two sign choices for the image of a unit source vector, but the least costly representative has a simple form. The least-displacing orientation-preserving choice is the direct rotation through theta. Its displacement singular values are both a, where a equals twice the sine of half theta. The orientation-reversing choices are reflections that send the source line onto the target line. Its displacement singular values are two and zero.

slides.title: The hidden assumption in the generalization
slides.lead: Imagine two independent principal planes, both with the same small angle theta.
body: The canonical direct rotation acts as a theta rotation on each of them. We might be tempted to say that any competing transporter must incur at least the same cost plane by plane. But the constraint on W is only that it maps the whole source subspace onto the whole target subspace. It does not require W to match each source principal vector with its canonical target partner. If the two angles coincide, the source and target carry internal rotational freedoms that can be coupled.

slides.title: Compare with Proposition four point three
slides.lead: Why does the squared theorem not prohibit this?
body: Consider two lists. The direct rotation may have four equal displacement singular values a. A competing orthogonal map may have two larger singular values b and two zeros. For the positive squares, the lists are four copies of a squared versus two copies of b squared and two zeros. It is possible that every cumulative sum for the squared direct list is no larger than the corresponding cumulative sum for the squared competitor list, while the total unsquared direct sum four a is larger than the competitor's two b. There is no contradiction.

slides.title: A universal lower bound that remains true
slides.lead: There is, nevertheless, a lower bound on every full transport.
body: Let P and Q be the source and target orthogonal projections. If W transports U to V, then Q equals W P W adjoint. Introduce the reflections J-P equal two P minus identity and J-Q equal two Q minus identity. Their difference is two times P minus Q. The conjugacy condition says J-Q W equals W J-P. Rearrange this identity. The difference of the two reflections, multiplied by W, is a commutator involving identity minus W and a reflection. By the triangle inequality and unitary invariance, the norm of that commutator is at most twice the norm of identity minus W.

slides.title: How to test the printed claim
slides.lead: A universal minimizing statement must survive one explicit admissible competitor and one valid unitarily invariant norm.
body: We can therefore choose trace norm, which is the sum of singular values. The simplest potential counterexample should have enough dimensions to mix at least two principal planes. Four real dimensions suffice. We will take two equal acute principal angles. Then we will write a concrete orthogonal competitor, compute its action on the source plane, verify the resulting principal angles, and compute both displacement singular-value lists. The explicit singular values give a strict numerical contradiction to the printed inequality, so the universal proposition is false.

slides.title: Close
slides.lead: The sixty-degree threshold is correct for the standard two-dimensional real comparison.
body: Proposition four point one remains valid for restricted displacement, and Proposition four point three remains valid for positive squared displacement. Neither theorem authorizes the universal unsquared ambient conclusion in higher dimension. The source of the failure is extra freedom in the full orthogonal transport fiber, especially the freedom to mix repeated principal-angle directions.
